## What it is

The organization's plan for detecting, handling, reporting and recovering from cybersecurity incidents, with the ten elements NIST SP 800-53 IR-8 requires.

## Preview (annotated)

:::note[Guidance]
This plan answers the ten questions IR-8a asks of an incident response plan; each section names the IR-8 item it meets. The handling sections follow the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 Functions, as [NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final) (April 2025) does: Detect, Respond and Recover for handling an incident, with preparation and improvement around them. Keep the plan short enough to use during an incident, and move step-by-step instructions into the [incident handling playbook](/templates/procedures/incident-handling-playbook/). The breach part of section 5 meets IR-8(1), which is in the Privacy baseline; a system that processes personally identifiable information needs it, and any organization that holds such information benefits from it.
:::

### 1. Purpose and scope

This plan is <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span>'s roadmap for its incident response capability: how incidents are detected, handled, reported and learned from (IR-8a.1). It applies to every system <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span> owns or operates, or that is operated on its behalf, and to everyone with access to those systems.

### 2. How incident response fits the organization

Incident response is part of <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span>'s security program and risk management. The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> works with system owners, who remain responsible for their systems during an incident, and with the contingency planning, business continuity and crisis communications functions when an incident affects operations (IR-8a.3).

The capability is sized for <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span>'s mission, size, structure and functions as follows: <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: how the capability is staffed and sourced, for example an internal team with a retained incident response provider for major incidents</span> (IR-8a.4).

### 3. Roles and responsibilities

Responsibility for incident response is designated to <span class="tpl-field tpl-param">Fill in: entities, personnel, or roles with designated responsibility for incident response <span class="tpl-typical">Typical: the incident response team, led by its designated lead</span></span> (IR-8a.10). The capability is organized as follows (IR-8a.2).

| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Chief Information Security Officer</span> | Owns this plan; declares major incidents; decides with legal counsel on outside notification; reports to senior leadership |
| Incident response lead | Leads the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span>; coordinates handling of each incident from declaration to closure |
| <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> | Analyzes, contains, eradicates and recovers from incidents; keeps the incident record |
| <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Security operations team</span> | Monitors for and triages events; escalates suspected incidents |
| <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">System owner</span> | Provides system knowledge and access; approves containment and recovery actions on their system |
| Legal counsel | Advises on evidence, notification duties and law enforcement contact |
| Communications | Prepares internal and external messages approved by the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Chief Information Security Officer</span> |
| <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Human resources office</span> | Supports incidents that involve personnel |
| All personnel | Report suspected incidents promptly and follow the team's instructions |

### 4. Reportable incidents

A reportable incident is any event that actually or imminently jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span>'s information or systems, or that violates security policy or acceptable use (IR-8a.5). Examples include malware infections, unauthorized access, lost or stolen devices with <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span> information, and data sent to the wrong recipient. When in doubt, report it.

The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> assigns each incident a severity, which sets the response time and who is informed.

| Severity | Description | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |

| High | <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: description</span> | <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: response time and escalation</span> |
| Moderate | <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: description</span> | <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: response time and escalation</span> |
| Low | <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: description</span> | <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: response time and escalation</span> |

Personnel report suspected incidents to the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> within <span class="tpl-field tpl-param">Fill in: time period for personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident response capability <span class="tpl-typical">Typical: 1 hour of discovery</span></span>, through <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: reporting channels, for example the service desk phone number and the incident report form</span>, and reports are recorded on the [incident report form](/templates/forms/incident-report-form/). The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> reports incident information to <span class="tpl-field tpl-param">Fill in: authorities to whom incident information is to be reported <span class="tpl-typical">Typical: senior leadership, legal counsel, and any regulator, customer or partner that law or contract requires be notified</span></span>.

<div class="tpl-federal">

#### Federal systems

Federal agencies notify the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) of incidents under FISMA (44 U.S.C. §§ 3553 and 3554). As of October 2026, the [CISA Federal Incident Notification Guidelines](https://www.cisa.gov/federal-incident-notification-guidelines) (effective April 1, 2017) require notification within one hour of the incident being identified by the agency's top-level incident response team, security operations center or IT department. Record the agency's reporting channel to CISA and who submits the report: <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: agency CISA reporting procedure and submitter</span>.

[OMB Memorandum M-25-04](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/M-25-04-Fiscal-Year-2025-Guidance-on-Federal-Information-Security-and-Privacy-Management-Requirements.pdf) (January 15, 2025), the most recent FISMA guidance memorandum as of October 2026, section X, defines a major incident and requires a major incident determination for any breach affecting the personally identifiable information of 100,000 or more people. Events unresolved after 72 hours of investigation are reported to CISA. A major incident is reported to CISA and the OMB Office of the Federal Chief Information Officer within 1 hour of the determination, and to the appropriate congressional committees and the Office of Inspector General within 7 days of the reasonable-basis determination. Use M-25-04's definition when major incidents are declared (section 3), and record who makes the determination and who sends each report: <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: officials who determine major incidents and report to OMB, CISA, Congress and the Office of Inspector General</span>.

</div>

#### Breaches involving personally identifiable information

A breach is an incident involving personally identifiable information: its loss of control, compromise, unauthorized disclosure or acquisition, or a similar occurrence where someone other than an authorized user accesses or potentially accesses it, or an authorized user does so for other than authorized purposes. Suspected breaches are reported like any other incident, in any medium or form, including paper, oral and electronic. The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> tells the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Senior privacy official</span> as soon as personally identifiable information is, or may be, involved, and the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Senior privacy official</span> leads the steps below, which section 5.8 of the incident handling playbook carries out (IR-8(1)).

| --- | --- |

| Assessing harm, embarrassment, inconvenience or unfairness to individuals, and how to mitigate it (IR-8(1)(b)) | The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Senior privacy official</span> weighs the sensitivity of the information, the number of individuals, whether it was actually accessed or used, and the context. Mitigation available: <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: for example credit monitoring, a call center, help replacing account numbers</span> |

<div class="tpl-federal">

##### Federal systems

[OMB Memorandum M-17-12](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/legacy_drupal_files/omb/memoranda/2017/m-17-12_0.pdf) (January 3, 2017), section VII, requires the senior agency official for privacy to develop a breach response plan as part of the agency's formal incident response plan; this section can serve as that plan once it covers each element section VII lists. Record the breach response team the head of the agency designates, which the senior agency official for privacy leads and which includes at least the CIO or designee, the senior agency information security officer, legal counsel, and legislative affairs and communications officials (section VII.A): <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: team members by title, and the criteria for convening the team</span>. The head of the agency makes the final decision on notifying individuals, on the senior agency official for privacy's advice (section VII.G). The senior agency official for privacy reviews the plan at the end of each fiscal year (section X.B) and convenes the team for a tabletop exercise at least annually (section X.A). For a breach that is a major incident under OMB M-25-04, section X, a supplemental report goes to Congress within 30 days of discovering the breach. As of October 2026.

</div>

### 6. Handling incidents

Handling follows the CSF 2.0 Functions. The [incident handling playbook](/templates/procedures/incident-handling-playbook/) holds the step-by-step instructions, with first steps for each common type of incident.

#### Detect

The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Security operations team</span> monitors alerts, logs and user reports; triages events; and escalates suspected incidents to the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span>, as the [log review procedure](/templates/procedures/log-review-procedure/) describes for findings in audit records. The team confirms whether an incident has occurred, declares it, assigns a severity and opens an incident record (IR-5).

#### Respond

The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> analyzes the incident to understand its scope and cause, contains it to limit damage, and eradicates its cause, coordinating each action with the affected <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">System owner</span>. It preserves evidence, keeps the incident record current, and coordinates communication and notification as section 5 describes.

#### Recover

The <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">System owner</span> restores affected systems and data, with the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> confirming they are clean and monitored for recurrence. Recovery that invokes a contingency plan follows that plan.

#### Improve

After each incident of <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: severity that requires a lessons-learned review, for example High or Critical</span>, the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Incident response team</span> holds a lessons-learned review within <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: time after closure, for example 10 business days</span>. Changes to procedures, training and testing that result are tracked to completion (IR-4c).

### 7. Sharing incident information

<span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span> shares incident information with <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: parties, for example sector information sharing organizations, suppliers involved in the incident, and law enforcement</span> when <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: conditions and who approves</span> (IR-8a.8). Suppliers of affected products or services receive the information they need to respond (IR-6(3)).

### 9. Resources and management support

Maintaining and maturing the capability requires <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: staff, tools, retained services and budget</span>, which the <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Senior leader</span> supports through <span class="tpl-field tpl-fill">Fill in: how resources are approved, for example the annual security budget</span> (IR-8a.7).

### 10. Training and testing

Incident response roles receive training on joining the role and at the interval the Incident Response Policy sets (IR-2). The capability is tested through exercises at the interval that policy sets, and the results feed section 6's improvement step (IR-3). The [tabletop exercise kit](/templates/plans/tabletop-exercise-kit/) holds the materials and the after-action report for each exercise. Where <span class="tpl-field tpl-org">Organization name</span> holds personally identifiable information, at least one exercise each year simulates a breach (IR-2(3)).
